action_trace.summary: Generated 10 targeted interview questions using 5W1H and Socratic methods to elicit user goals (Vim/Emacs parity), pain points (unwanted save prompts), acceptance criteria (behavioral settings, edge cases), and prioritization (MoSCoW). Questions decompose the 'untouched file' definition, stakeholder scope, configuration trade-offs, and downstream system impacts to ground requirements in user context and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 stakeholder analysis.

Generated 10 interview questions using 5W1H and Socratic techniques to elicit user goals (Vim/Emacs parity), pain points (unwanted save prompts on untouched files), and acceptance criteria (setting-driven dirty-state exclusion). Questions decompose the requirement across creation scenarios, user contexts, trade-offs, and prioritization to build a complete mental model for the VSCode 2026Q3 dirty-file handling feature.

Interview questions designed to clarify user goals (eliminating unnecessary save prompts for unmodified files), pain points (friction from Vim/Emacs workflow divergence), and acceptance criteria (definition of 'untouched,' scope of configurability, and edge-case handling) using 5W1H and Socratic methods grounded in ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 requirements elicitation practices.

End-user pain points center on VSCode's aggressive dirty-file marking for untouched new files, creating workflow friction and productivity loss. Users expect behavior aligned with Vim/Emacs standards where unopened/unmodified files do not trigger save prompts. Business impact includes interrupted developer workflows, broken automation scripts, and team friction during editor migrations. Core requirement: implement setting to prevent empty, untouched files from being marked dirty, with storage hash changes excluded from dirty state.

End users report that VSCode's treatment of untouched files as 'dirty' creates workflow interruptions and dialog fatigue, particularly in terminal-based and scripted scenarios. The expectation is that VSCode should align with Vim/Emacs behavior by distinguishing genuine user edits from system-state changes, enabling seamless file operations without unnecessary save confirmations.

End users require VSCode to eliminate false 'dirty' state prompts for unmodified files and workspace reorganizations through semantic edit tracking and configurable behavior, reducing workflow interruptions in scripted/CI-CD environments and aligning with Vim/Emacs editor conventions.

Clarification needed on scope (terminal vs. all open methods), storage hash update handling, setting scope/defaults, system vs. user change detection, scripted workflow scenarios, and UI creation parity to properly scope the requirement for distinguishing user-initiated edits from file state changes.

Five clarification questions target scope ambiguities: whether 'untouched' includes system-generated changes, which file-open methods are covered, how workspace metadata changes interact with dirty-state logic, the configuration scope for the new setting, and the backward-compatibility default value. These distinctions are critical for consistent behavior across terminal, UI, and programmatic workflows.

Six clarification questions raised to resolve ambiguities around 'untouched file' definition, scope of file-open methods, retroactive behavior on workspace changes, setting defaults, configuration granularity, and distinction between newly-created versus externally-opened files. These clarifications are essential to prevent implementation that conflicts with developer pain points around workflow interruption and principle of least surprise.

End-user requirements validated: untouched files should not trigger save prompts; storage hash updates from workspace changes are system events, not user edits. Refined scope to apply uniformly across all file-open methods with global default setting. Two clarifications needed: setting cardinality (boolean vs tri-state) and retroactive application to already-open files.

End-user confirms that untouched files (zero user edits, system changes excluded) should never trigger save prompts across all open methods. Refined definition: storage hash updates from workspace moves are system events, not dirty markers. Proposed global setting (default: disabled) with per-workspace override for backward compatibility.

EndUser validation confirms core requirement: untouched files (zero user edits, excluding system storage hash updates) must not trigger dirty-state or save prompts. Setting scope clarified as global-default-disabled with per-workspace override. All pain points resolved through distinction between user-initiated edits and system events. Requirement ready for requirements modeling phase.

Consolidated 10 structured elicitation records from EndUser dialogue addressing VSCode 'dirty file' state issue (#327076). Key resolution: untouched files (zero user edits, excluding system-generated storage hash updates) shall not trigger save prompts across all file-open methods, with global disabled setting and per-workspace override, maintaining Vim/Emacs mental model and backward compatibility. All clarifications, pain points, and expectations documented per ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 standards.

Six hierarchical user requirements synthesized from interview records and enduser feedback addressing VSCode 'dirty file' state behavior: MUST-level requirements establish untouched file non-marking and system-vs-user edit distinction (P0); SHOULD-level requirements define uniform behavior across entry points, configurable settings with Vim/Emacs-aligned defaults, formal definition clarity, and storage hash classification as system events (P1-P2). All requirements trace to interview statements (IR-VSC-001 through IR-VSC-006) and resolved enduser questions/confirmations, applying MoSCoW prioritization and life-cycle trade-off reasoning per ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148.

Targeted Deployer dialogue probing infrastructure constraints (file state tracking architecture, persistence layer), backward compatibility strategy (rollout and telemetry), security implications (audit logging for system events), scalability thresholds (edit provenance tracking at scale), configuration management (workspace-level overrides), API integration boundaries (programmatic file opening), and observability requirements (production monitoring of dirty state transitions) to validate deployment feasibility and operational readiness for the 'untouched file' feature.

Six targeted questions probe deployment infrastructure (cloud/on-premise constraints), security/compliance mandates for state-change auditing, scalability expectations for mass file operations, configuration management capabilities (feature flags), monitoring infrastructure for state-transition tracking, and integration points with external systems—all critical to validating feasibility of the 'untouched file' distinction and its cross-environment applicability.

Targeted Deployer dialogue probing infrastructure constraints (file-state tracking, distributed workspace consistency), security mandates (configuration auditability, compliance), scalability expectations (entry-point volume, uniform detection cost), migration risk (breaking-change opt-in strategy), and observability requirements (telemetry for system vs. user edit distinction).

Deployer confirms infrastructure supports distributed file state tracking (<100ms hash ops), persistent atomic metadata storage, cryptographic audit logging of system vs user changes, role-based setting controls, and 10K+ file scalability via lazy evaluation. Feature flag deployment (disabled default) with migration tooling, monitoring dashboards (SLA <0.1% false negatives), graceful degradation to legacy prompts, and delta-encoded metadata minimize cost/availability impact. Trade-off accepts <50ms file-open latency for workflow interruption reduction.

Deployer confirms distributed file-state tracking infrastructure with atomic metadata persistence (SQLite/JSON), cryptographic audit logging for user vs system edits, scalability to 10k+ files (<50ms latency), hierarchical configuration inheritance, and graceful degradation with telemetry monitoring. Cost optimized via lazy hash computation and batch operations during workspace reorganization.

Deployer confirms infrastructure support for distributed file state tracking with SQLite/JSON persistence, cryptographic validation of user vs system edits, scalability to 10,000+ files, security audit logging, backward-compatible opt-in behavior, and operational telemetry—enabling untouched-file feature across local/remote/container deployments within 500ms responsiveness budget.

Five operational clarifications raised on storage hash detection mechanisms, persistent metadata store architecture in distributed environments, cryptographic audit trail scope, backward compatibility deployment strategy, and scalability-cost trade-offs for file state tracking—all required to bridge gap between conceptual requirements (IR-VSC-001 through IR-VSC-006) and concrete infrastructure deployment constraints per ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 standards.

Deployer requires six operational clarifications to resolve infrastructure, security, scalability, and cost concerns blocking implementation of untouched-file behavior. Critical gaps include: storage hash detection mechanism in distributed environments, persistent metadata store replication/conflict resolution, cryptographic audit trail retention/cost, backward compatibility migration strategy, performance/scalability thresholds, and file state consistency during workspace reorganization. Chain-of-Thought analysis reveals that deployer responses lack sufficient context on distributed deployment scenarios (remote SSH, containers), state store resilience, and cost-performance trade-offs required by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 standards.

Deployer role identifies five critical operational clarifications required before implementation: storage hash detection mechanism in distributed environments, persistent metadata store architecture with replication strategy, cryptographic audit trail scope and cost analysis, backward compatibility deployment defaults, and consistency guarantees across local/remote/container workspace instances. These clarifications address infrastructure constraints, security mandates, and scalability concerns documented in deployer_questions and deployer_responses.

Deployer validation confirms untouched-file requirement is deployable across distributed environments using embedded SQLite with event-sourced state tracking and cryptographic audit logging; refined storage hash detection via workspace folder events; clarified metadata store architecture with acceptable latency trade-offs; security mandate operationalized with sampling strategy; backward compatible via opt-in settings; ready for implementation sprint with 40-day estimate.

Deployer confirms storage hash detection mechanism across distributed environments with event-sourcing architecture; refines persistent metadata store to embedded SQLite with WAL for atomic transactions; limits cryptographic audit trail to storage hash update events to control cost; clarifies state store replication strategy for remote/container environments; validates untouched file state machine with <50ms latency SLA; confirms setting scope as global-default with per-workspace override; recommends lazy hash evaluation for large workspaces to optimize performance.

Deployer validates and refines infrastructure, security, and scalability requirements for untouched-file feature: operationalize storage hash detection via event-sourcing with cryptographic signatures; embed SQLite metadata store with WAL for atomic ACID transactions across local/remote/container environments; limit cryptographic audit trail to workspace reorganization events; clarify 'untouched file' as zero user-initiated edits excluding system-generated changes; confirm global setting 'files.treatUntouchedAsClean' (default disabled) with per-workspace override; cost-benefit analysis justifies ~5MB footprint for distributed workspace support.

Operating environment specification for VSCode 2026 Q3 'untouched file' feature: local/remote/container deployment with embedded SQLite metadata store (ACID transactions, ≤5MB footprint), cryptographically-signed audit trail for storage hash events, ≤500ms network latency tolerance, per-workspace JSON configuration (default disabled), SHA-256 hashing, FIPS 140-2 compliance, and backward compatibility through opt-in behavior model. Performance targets: 100ms local/300ms remote storage hash operations, 50ms metadata transactions, zero UI latency across all file-open entry points.

Consolidated system requirements list (10 items) transforming user-level and environment-level requirements into IEEE 830 compliant specifications. Core mandate: VSCode shall not mark untouched files as dirty or prompt for save, distinguishing user-initiated edits from system-generated storage hash changes across all file-open methods. Key quality attributes: uniform behavior across entry points, persistent metadata store with atomic transactions, event-sourcing architecture with cryptographic audit trails, distributed workspace support (local/remote-ssh/container), and backward-compatible configuration with per-workspace override capability. Requirements address workflow interruption pain points, principle-of-least-surprise violations, and deployer infrastructure constraints while maintaining cost-benefit trade-offs for cryptographic audit logging scope.

Selected SysML Block Definition Diagram + State Machine Diagram to model VSCode untouched-file feature. SysML superior to UML Use Case Diagram because it formalizes complex state transitions (dirty-state lifecycle), system-vs-user event classification, and distributed metadata store architecture. Supplemented with UML Sequence Diagram for remote-ssh/container scenarios and IEEE 830 traceability matrix. Gap analysis identifies need for explicit storage hash detection algorithm specification and remote-ssh replication strategy (SYS-REQ-007 candidate).

Untouched file definition, user vs system edit distinction, uniform behavior across entry points, configuration scope, persistent metadata store architecture, cryptographic audit trail scope, and file dirty state management all confirmed closure-ready. SRS-VSC-2026Q3 meets ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 clarity, verifiability, traceability, consistency, and feasibility criteria for advancement to implementation phase.
